(2) Excessive dwelling unit density. The average density of 23 units per acre is in itself a realistic density for some types of residential construction. It is in fact close to the density that the Randolph Plan expects to provide (20 units per acre expected replacement) in some areas. The basic differences are not in the units per acre average but in the types of residential structures, their lot coverage, and the open space provided. Structures in the Randolph Area are one and two stories with few exceptions. Proposed structures are also one and two stories, with the possible exception of a four story elderly housing development. Excessive dwelling unit density is exhibited in a number of residences that are spacially inadequate to house the number of people living there. Many one, two, and three bedroom units house much larger family units and are overcrowded.
(3) Many structures have been converted to accommodate larger numbers of people and are incompatible in family dwelling areas. The intrusion of roominghouses into single family areas and the conversion of single family homes into multiple units contributes to these incompatible uses. The pressures of insufficient housing make residents accept what is available and rents are reflected by what the market will bear.
(4) Obsolete building types, such as large residences or other buildings which through the lack of maintenance have a blighting influence through the community. Many buildings are residential conversions as mentioned above that have fallen in decay from overcrowded conditions and the lack of maintenance.
(5) Unsafe, congested, poorly designed, or otherwise deficient streets are located through the project. Many of these streets were originally designed for much smaller densities and single family rather than multiple family uses. Many structures converted to increased dwelling unit capacity have not provided additional offstreet parking. Many alleys are one lane dirt or gravel lanes that gather litter and accumulated trash. Little parking is provided off the alleys in high density areas.
